Basal metabolic rate measurements in the Southern pocket gopher (Thomomys umbrinus) have been obtained through respirometry trials on captive individuals. When maintained at a thermoneutral body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], the maximum resting oxygen consumption was recorded at 72.3 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 72.3 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This metabolic rate, reflecting the species' fossorial lifestyle, is consistent with values reported for other Thomomys species of comparable size. The high energetic cost of digging through compacted soils likely contributes to this elevated metabolism relative to surface-dwelling rodents. Adjustments to metabolic output during periods of inactivity further illustrate the energetic trade-offs inherent to a life spent excavating extensive subterranean tunnel systems in search of forage.

Neonatal development in Thomomys umbrinus begins with a relatively brief gestation period of 19 days [tg = 19 days] at a sustained core temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. Newborn pups emerge weighing approximately 2.5 grams [Wwb = approximately 2.5 grams], a modest birth mass typical of altricial rodents. These altricial neonates are entirely dependent on maternal care during the early postnatal phase. The suckling juveniles remain in the natal burrow system, nursing continuously as they undergo rapid mass gain under the insulated subterranean conditions that buffer extreme surface temperatures. Weaning occurs relatively early compared to other geomyid rodents, with nutritional independence achieved at 38 days after birth [tx = 38 days after birth] under these same thermoneutral conditions at a temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C].

Following weaning, the young gophers disperse to establish their own burrow systems. Sexual maturation is reached considerably later, with puberty occurring at 319 days after birth [tp = 319 days after birth] at a core body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This extended juvenile period allows for complete skeletal development and the excavation of an extensive burrow network necessary for adult survival.

Adult body size in Thomomys umbrinus exhibits moderate sexual dimorphism, with females attaining a maximum recorded mass of 120 grams [Wwi = 120 grams] in wild populations. Males, by contrast, reach a larger ultimate body mass of 180 grams [Wwi = 180 grams], a difference likely linked to intrasexual competition for territories. These asymptotic masses are consistent with the species' position within the Thomomys genus and reflect the constraints of a subterranean existence. Breeding occurs throughout much of the year in favorable habitats, with reproductively active adults showing physiological adaptations for prolonged underground energy expenditure.

Female Southern pocket gophers produce litters of 4 to 5 pups per parturition [N_R_i = 4 to 5 pups per parturition] and typically complete 2 litters each year [F_R_i = 2 litters each year] under optimal conditions. Maximum longevity in this species is approximately 6 years [am = approximately 6 years] at a core body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], as inferred from captive records of the congeneric species Thomomys bottae. This lifespan, while modest for a small mammal, accommodates multiple breeding seasons given the relatively early onset of reproduction. The oldest documented individuals exhibit reduced metabolic output, consistent with the onset of reproductive senescence common among fossorial rodents.
